text: Triggers: record and scheduled. The trigger is the single most consequential choice you make when designing a flow, because it decides when the flow runs, how often, and on what. Flow Designer gives you two real options, and getting the wrong one is the most common way a new flow misbehaves.

A record trigger fires when a record on a chosen table is Created, Updated, Created or Updated, or optionally Deleted. You pick the table, then narrow it with a condition — the same condition-builder pattern you already used for Business Rules and ACLs. Without a condition, a trigger set to Created on Incident fires on every single new Incident, which is rarely what you actually want.

A scheduled trigger doesn't watch for a record change at all — it fires on a time-based schedule: daily, weekly, or a repeating interval. It's the same underlying idea as the Scheduled Jobs from an earlier course, just expressed natively inside Flow Designer. It's the right choice for a nightly cleanup flow or a weekly digest — automation that isn't reacting to anything specific.

The real question every time: should this run because something just happened, or because time passed? "When a Change gets approved" is a record trigger. "Every morning at 7am" is a scheduled trigger. Mix them up, and a real-time request sits unprocessed until the next scheduled run, or you're forcing a reaction out of data that didn't actually change.
Record trigger to react, scheduled trigger to run on a timer. Next up: putting both trigger types to work by building your first complete flow, from trigger to activation.
